questions.q: Classify: 'Although it rained, the match continued.'
questions.a: Complex — 'although' subordinates the first clause. A wrong answer 'compound' reveals the student classifies by clause COUNT alone, ignoring that the joiner type (subordinator vs coordinator) is the actual diagnostic.

questions.q: Make it simple: 'He was tired, so he went to bed.'
questions.a: 'Being tired, he went to bed' (or 'Tired, he went to bed'). A wrong answer 'He was tired and went to bed' keeps two finite verbs — the student joined clauses but never reduced the count, so the sentence is still compound.

questions.q: Is this legal? 'She loves maths, she practises daily.'
questions.a: No — comma splice; needs 'and' (compound), 'because' with order flip (complex), or a full stop. A wrong answer accepting it reveals the student believes a comma has conjunctive power — the single most common punctuation-structure error.

questions.q: ______ move meaning between these containers — 'Being tired, she slept' ≡ 'She was tired, so she slept' ≡ 'Because she was tired, she slept.'

Fill in the blank: Sentence structure is about clause count and dependence: simple = one finite verb, compound = independent clauses joined by ______ (and/but/or/yet/so/for), complex = one main + subordinate clause(s) joined by because/although/which/when/that.
Fill in the blank: Take one meaning — 'tired → slept' — and pour it into three ______.
What is Sentence structure? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Sentence structure is about clause count and dependence: simple = one finite verb, compound = independent clauses joined by coordinators (and/but/or/yet/so/for), complex = one main + subordinate clause(s) joined by because/although/which/when/that.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Sentence structure?
questions.a: Students call any long sentence 'complex', miss that 'and/but' between two full clauses is compound not complex, and write comma splices ('She was tired, she slept') believing a comma can join clauses.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student counts clauses correctly, identifies the connector type each structure needs, transforms among all three forms preserving meaning, and punctuates each correctly (comma-splice recognition).
